verdict: OK to lend in Daman plastics and rubber processing, but only to converters with pass-through pricing and verified raw-material cover; avoid units still shut or single-supplier dependent.
title: Daman Plastics & Rubber Processing: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**A Daman plastics unit buys polymer granules, runs them through extruders, moulders or recycling lines, and sells converted parts to nearby industrial and consumer buyers.** Cash turns on the spread between granule cost and the price the buyer accepts, not on volume alone. Granules are the dominant input cost, so the whole credit story is whether the unit can reprice when resin moves. [1] says around 25% of Daman plastic units shut temporarily after raw material prices surged. That is the fact that governs this note.

## Where cash and value sit now
**Value sits with converters who hold firm order books and can pass resin increases through; cash leaks in inventory and receivables.** The working-capital cycle is the time to convert net current assets into cash, and a longer cycle means more funding need [10]. So when a proposal lands, check the receivable days against the buyer mix; if receivables stretch while resin prices rise, ask for the price-revision clause in the supply contract. Peer results show the demand side is not the problem: Supreme Industries reports sales tonnage up 19% YoY and operating profit up 45% YoY [6], and Apcotex reports H1 revenue up 44% YoY with Q2 margin pressure from inventory losses and freight [7]. **Inventory losses, not weak demand, are the live risk.**

## The growth opportunity to pursue
**Pursue converters tied to recycling and reclaim, and units with diversified granule suppliers.** GRP Ltd reports total income up 26% YoY with EBITDA margin at 11% [4], and guides reclaim volume growth to mid-teens in FY27 [5]. Manika Plastech shows the safe profile: about 84% of FY25 raw material from its top five suppliers, gearing down to 0.66x as on March 31, 2026 from 0.86x [11]. So when a proposal lands, check supplier concentration; if one supplier exceeds the majority of purchases, ask for a second-source plan before sanction. **Avoid units still in the 25% shutdown group [1] and any borrower whose only edge is cheap resin.**

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the resin cycle, not the balance sheet.** Keep working-capital limits sized to the verified cycle [10], take monthly stock statements and a monthly granule purchase register, and require a Trust and Retention Account where cash flow is parked against the forthcoming obligation, as lenders do in monitored accounts [8]. Take stock and receivables ageing every month, and a quarterly confirmation of supplier terms. **Price the limit to the cycle, not to last year's turnover.**

## Early-warning signs
- Monthly stock statement (monthly): inventory days rise while sales are flat -> cut limit and ask for fresh orders.
- Granule purchase register (monthly): single-supplier share climbs -> seek second source or reduce exposure.
- Fire-safety inspection (quarterly): a plastic-company fire spread to three neighbouring units in Dadra [3] -> insist on current fire compliance before renewal.
- Receivables ageing (monthly): top-buyer days cross agreed limit -> move to cash-backed terms.

**Local sources are thin on Daman-specific numbers beyond the shutdown report [1]; the rest rests on first principles and peer results.**
